title: Infectious Musculoskeletal Diseases
subject: Musculoskeletal System (MUSC)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter explains how bacteria and one parasite reach joints, bone, fascia, and muscle, why each tissue responds as it does, and how laboratory and imaging findings reflect those responses. It covers septic arthritis and synovial fluid analysis, necrotizing fasciitis, hematogenous and contiguous osteomyelitis, dry, wet, and gas gangrene, pyomyositis, and trichinellosis. Board questions usually give a host (a child, a person with diabetes, an injection drug user, a patient with sickle cell disease) and a tissue, then ask for the organism, the route of spread, the key toxin, or the meaning of a lab value. Anatomy of the blood supply explains most of the answers.
prerequisites: Patterns of necrosis: coagulative, liquefactive, and caseous (general pathology)
Acute inflammation: neutrophil recruitment, proteases, and cytokines such as IL-1 and TNF
Long bone anatomy: epiphysis, physis, metaphysis, diaphysis, and periosteum (MS bone units)
Gram stain, oxygen requirements, and major virulence factors of staphylococci, streptococci, and clostridia
Synovial joint structure and the composition of articular cartilage

connections.how: Toxins such as Clostridium perfringens alpha toxin and streptococcal superantigens explain tissue destruction and shock.
Superantigens, complement deficiency in recurrent Neisseria infection, and Th2 responses with eosinophilia in helminth infection all appear in this chapter.
Neuropathy, vascular disease, and impaired neutrophil function make diabetes the leading host factor for foot osteomyelitis, gangrene, and type I necrotizing fasciitis.
Sickle cell disease favors Salmonella osteomyelitis, and clostridial alpha toxin causes intravascular hemolysis.
Synovial fluid analysis separates septic arthritis from gout, pseudogout, and rheumatoid arthritis, which can coexist with infection.

terms.def: Infection of a joint space, most often bacterial, that produces purulent synovial fluid and rapid cartilage destruction.
Infection of bone and marrow, reached through the blood, from a neighboring infection, or by direct inoculation.
The flared region of a long bone between the shaft and the growth plate, where blood flow slows in looping vessels.
A fragment of dead bone separated from living bone by infection and loss of blood supply.
A sleeve of new reactive bone laid down by lifted periosteum around a sequestrum.
A localized, walled-off bone abscess surrounded by sclerotic bone, typical of subacute osteomyelitis.
Rapidly spreading infection of the subcutaneous fascia that thromboses perforating vessels and kills the overlying tissue.
A toxin that links MHC class II on antigen-presenting cells to the T cell receptor outside the peptide groove, activating many T cells at once.

A phospholipase C (lecithinase) that hydrolyzes membrane phospholipids, lysing muscle cells, red cells, and platelets.
Bacterial abscess within skeletal muscle, usually Staphylococcus aureus in a large muscle of the thigh, buttock, or iliopsoas.
A skeletal muscle cell remodeled by an encysting Trichinella larva into a capsule with its own new capillary network.

sections.title: Septic arthritis: routes, organisms, and risk factors

blocks.text: Most septic arthritis is hematogenous. The synovial membrane is richly vascular, its capillaries are fenestrated, and the synovial lining has no limiting basement membrane, so bacteria carried in the blood during a transient bacteremia cross easily into the joint. Synovial fluid then supports their growth. Less often, organisms are inoculated directly by joint injection, arthroscopy or surgery, a penetrating injury, or an animal or human bite, or spread from adjacent osteomyelitis. Infection is usually monoarticular, and the knee is the joint most often involved.

Once bacteria are in the joint, neutrophils pour in. Their proteases, reactive oxygen species, and the cytokines IL-1 and TNF, together with bacterial toxins, activate matrix metalloproteinases in chondrocytes and synovium that degrade proteoglycan and then collagen. Articular cartilage has no blood supply and little capacity for repair, so matrix lost within the first few days is lost permanently. A tense effusion can also compress the blood supply of the bone end; in a child's hip this can cause avascular necrosis of the femoral head.

Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause overall. In sexually active young adults, Neisseria gonorrhoeae is the classic cause and produces disseminated gonococcal infection, either a purulent monoarthritis or a triad of migratory polyarthralgia, tenosynovitis (wrists, hands, ankles), and sparse pustular skin lesions. Gonococci are fastidious, so joint fluid cultures are often negative and cultures of the urethra, cervix, pharynx, or rectum are more often positive. Recurrent disseminated Neisseria infection points to deficiency of the terminal complement components C5 to C9, which form the membrane attack complex.

Risk factors either damage the joint or impair host defense. Rheumatoid arthritis combines abnormal, inflamed synovium with immunosuppressive therapy, and its flare can hide infection. Prosthetic joints carry foreign material on which bacteria form biofilm that resists phagocytosis. Injection drug use causes repeated bacteremia and favors unusual joints such as the sternoclavicular and sacroiliac joints. Diabetes impairs neutrophil function. Older age, chronic kidney disease, gout, and joint trauma also raise risk.

sections.title: Synovial fluid analysis in the acute hot swollen joint

blocks.text: Normal synovial fluid is a plasma ultrafiltrate to which synovial fibroblast-like (type B) cells add hyaluronic acid and lubricin. Hyaluronic acid makes the fluid viscous, and the fluid is clear and nearly acellular (under about 200 WBC/mm3). Arthrocentesis is the key test in a hot swollen joint because it separates three categories that look alike at the bedside.

As inflammation increases, neutrophils enter and their enzymes depolymerize hyaluronic acid, so the fluid becomes thinner, cloudier, and more cellular. White cell count and neutrophil percentage rise along a continuum, so the cutoffs are guides rather than absolute lines. Neutrophils and bacteria consume glucose, so in septic fluid glucose falls well below the serum level. A Gram stain is positive in only about half of nongonococcal infections and fewer gonococcal ones, so a negative stain does not exclude infection; culture is the definitive test.

blocks.title: Synovial fluid categories
rows: Rheumatoid arthritis, gout, pseudogout, reactive arthritis, Lyme arthritis
blocks.caption: Counts overlap at the edges: gonococcal and partially treated infections can fall below 50,000, and severe gout can exceed it.

blocks.text: Crystals are identified by compensated polarized light microscopy. Monosodium urate crystals of gout are needle shaped and strongly negatively birefringent, so they appear yellow when aligned parallel to the slow axis of the red compensator. Calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystals of pseudogout are rhomboid and weakly positively birefringent, so they appear blue when parallel. Crystals prove a crystal arthropathy but do not exclude infection, because the two can coexist and an infected joint can shed crystals; a very high count is treated as possible infection until culture results return. A bloody effusion suggests trauma, fracture, a bleeding disorder such as hemophilia, or pigmented villonodular synovitis.

blocks.title: Crystals under polarized light
blocks.caption: Color reverses when the crystal is turned perpendicular to the compensator axis.

blocks.title: Reading a joint aspirate
blocks.text: A 70-year-old man with known gout has a hot, swollen knee and a temperature of 38.6 degrees C (101.5 degrees F). The aspirate is opaque, with 85,000 WBC/mm3, 92% neutrophils, glucose much lower than serum, a negative Gram stain, and needle-shaped negatively birefringent crystals. The crystals confirm urate, but they do not explain the picture. A count above 50,000 with over 90% neutrophils and low glucose places the fluid in the septic range, and Gram stains are negative in about half of septic joints. The correct reading is possible septic arthritis coexisting with gout until culture is negative.

Necrotizing fasciitis is infection of the subcutaneous tissue and superficial fascia that spreads along fascial planes faster than the skin changes reveal. The superficial fascia is relatively poorly vascularized and offers little resistance to spread. Perforating vessels pass through it to supply the overlying skin, and as bacteria and their toxins thrombose these vessels, the skin above becomes ischemic. Cutaneous nerves running in the same plane are first inflamed and later destroyed.

blocks.title: From fascial infection to visible necrosis
steps: Organisms enter through a minor wound or surgical site
Enzymes and toxins spread along the superficial fascia
Perforating vessels to the skin thrombose
Skin becomes ischemic: dusky, then bullae, then necrosis
Cutaneous nerves die: early pain, later anesthesia
Toxins and cytokines cause sepsis or toxic shock
blocks.caption: The deep infection leads; the skin findings lag behind it.

blocks.text: This sequence explains the clinical signs. Pain is out of proportion to the exam because the deep infection is extensive while the skin still looks only mildly red. Edema and tenderness extend beyond the margin of erythema. As ischemia progresses, the skin turns gray or violaceous and forms hemorrhagic bullae, and later the area may become numb as nerves die. Gas-producing organisms cause crepitus. Liquefied fascia gives thin gray fluid, foul when anaerobes are present, rather than true pus. Systemic toxicity (fever, tachycardia, hypotension, confusion) and laboratory signs such as marked leukocytosis, hyponatremia, and a raised creatine kinase when muscle is involved reflect the bacterial burden and toxin load.

Type I is polymicrobial: anaerobes (Bacteroides, Peptostreptococcus, sometimes Clostridium) with facultative organisms such as Enterobacteriaceae and non-group A streptococci. Aerobes consume oxygen and lower the redox potential, which lets anaerobes grow, and mixed fermentation produces gas. It occurs in diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, obesity, and after abdominal or perineal surgery. Fournier gangrene is type I infection of the perineum and genitalia, spreading along Colles fascia, Scarpa fascia, and the dartos layer. Type II is monomicrobial Streptococcus pyogenes (group A), sometimes with S. aureus, and can strike healthy people of any age after minor trauma, varicella lesions, or injection drug use. Its virulence factors include antiphagocytic M protein, hyaluronidase, streptokinase, the cysteine protease SpeB, and the pyrogenic exotoxins SpeA and SpeC. These exotoxins are superantigens: they bind MHC class II and the T cell receptor variable beta region outside the peptide groove, activating up to about 20% of T cells and releasing IL-2, TNF, and IL-1, which produces streptococcal toxic shock syndrome.

blocks.title: Type I versus type II necrotizing fasciitis
rows: Streptococcus pyogenes, with or without S. aureus
blocks.caption: Both types share pain out of proportion, rapid spread, bullae, and systemic toxicity.

blocks.predict: Why can a patient with necrotizing fasciitis have severe pain on the first day but a numb, dusky area two days later?
blocks.explain: Early on, inflamed cutaneous nerves in the fascial plane signal intense pain while the skin still has its blood supply. As perforating vessels thrombose, both skin and nerves die, so the area darkens and loses sensation.

sections.title: Routes of osteomyelitis: metaphyseal seeding in children, contiguous and vertebral disease in adults

blocks.text: Bacteria reach bone by three routes: hematogenous seeding, contiguous spread from an adjacent soft tissue infection, and direct inoculation through an open fracture, surgery, or a puncture. Age decides which route dominates, because bone blood supply changes with growth.

In children, hematogenous osteomyelitis localizes to the metaphysis of rapidly growing long bones, most often the distal femur and proximal tibia. Branches of the nutrient artery run to the growth plate and turn back in sharp loops that empty into wide venous sinusoids. Flow there slows and becomes turbulent, the sinusoidal lining has gaps, and phagocytic activity is low, so circulating bacteria such as S. aureus lodge and multiply. Minor trauma that causes a small hematoma in this region may add a nidus.

blocks.title: Why the child's metaphysis is seeded
steps: Transient bacteremia carries S. aureus to bone
Nutrient artery branches loop at the growth plate
Flow slows in wide metaphyseal venous sinusoids
Gaps in the lining and few phagocytes let bacteria lodge
Abscess forms; pus spreads through the cortex
blocks.caption: The growth plate usually stops spread toward the epiphysis after infancy.

blocks.text: The growth plate shapes what happens next. In infants under about 18 months, vessels still cross the physis, so infection can reach the epiphysis and the joint. In older children the avascular physis acts as a barrier, so pus spreads outward through the thin metaphyseal cortex and lifts the loosely attached periosteum. Where the metaphysis lies inside the joint capsule (proximal femur, proximal humerus, radial neck, and distal lateral tibia), pus can enter the joint and cause septic arthritis. After the physis closes in adults, long bone hematogenous infection is uncommon, and when it occurs it can reach the epiphysis and joint.

In adults, hematogenous osteomyelitis is mostly vertebral, usually lumbar, seeded from urinary tract infection, endocarditis, intravascular catheters, or injection drug use. Adult intervertebral discs are avascular, so bacteria settle in the richly supplied vertebral endplate, then destroy the disc and cross to the neighboring endplate. The result is spondylodiscitis: two adjacent vertebral bodies and the disc between them, often with back pain, fever, and risk of epidural or psoas abscess. Children's discs still have a blood supply, so isolated discitis is possible. Tuberculous spondylitis (Pott disease) favors the lower thoracic spine, often spares the disc early, spreads under the anterior longitudinal ligament to several levels, forms cold paraspinal abscesses, and can collapse vertebrae into an angular gibbus.

Contiguous osteomyelitis is typical of the diabetic foot. Sensory neuropathy removes protective pain, motor neuropathy deforms the foot and creates pressure points over the metatarsal heads, and peripheral artery disease and poor neutrophil function slow healing. An ulcer deepens until it reaches bone; bone felt with a sterile probe at the ulcer base strongly suggests osteomyelitis. These infections are polymicrobial.

blocks.title: Osteomyelitis by setting
rows: S. aureus; K. kingae under about 4 years
Hematogenous; may cross physis to joint
S. aureus, group B streptococci, Escherichia coli
S. aureus, gram-negative bacilli from urinary source
Polymicrobial: S. aureus, streptococci, gram-negatives, anaerobes
blocks.caption: S. aureus remains common in every group, so the special organisms are additions, not replacements.

blocks.text: In sickle cell disease, bone infarcts provide dead tissue, bowel microinfarcts allow Salmonella into the blood, and functional asplenia impairs clearance of bacteria from the blood, so Salmonella osteomyelitis is characteristic.

sections.title: Osteomyelitis: pathology, laboratory and imaging findings, and complications

blocks.text: Bone is rigid, so inflammation inside it has nowhere to expand. Neutrophils and edema raise pressure in the marrow cavity and Haversian canals, compressing vessels and causing ischemic necrosis within about 48 hours. Pus that reaches the surface lifts the periosteum, which in children is loosely attached, and strips away the outer blood supply to the cortex. Bone that has lost both its medullary and periosteal supply dies; histologically its lacunae are empty of osteocytes.

blocks.title: From abscess to chronic osteomyelitis
steps: Pus raises pressure inside rigid bone
Intraosseous vessels collapse; bone becomes ischemic
Pus lifts the periosteum, cutting the cortical supply
Dead bone separates as a sequestrum
Lifted periosteum lays down an involucrum
Avascular sequestrum harbors bacteria; sinus tracts drain
blocks.caption: Dead bone without blood flow cannot be reached by neutrophils, which is why infection persists.

blocks.text: Osteoclasts at the margin of dead bone resorb the interface and free the fragment as a sequestrum. Meanwhile the lifted periosteum, still alive, lays down a shell of reactive woven bone, the involucrum, around the infected segment. Openings in the involucrum through which pus escapes are called cloacae, and pus that continues to the skin forms a chronic draining sinus tract. Because the sequestrum has no blood flow, bacteria in its canals and in biofilm are protected from neutrophils and circulating antibody, so chronic infection can smolder for years and flare after quiescent periods.

A Brodie abscess is the subacute form: a small abscess, usually in the tibial metaphysis of a child or young adult, walled off by a rim of sclerotic reactive bone. It causes localized aching pain, often worse at night, with few systemic signs, and appears radiographically as a lucent lesion with a sclerotic margin.

blocks.caption: Imaging shows inflammation; only bone culture proves the organism.

blocks.text: Complications follow from the pathology. Chronic osteomyelitis with a draining sinus develops in a minority of patients, especially with diabetes, vascular disease, or retained hardware. Squamous cell carcinoma (Marjolin ulcer) can arise in the epithelium lining a chronic sinus tract after years to decades of repeated injury and repair; a change in drainage, bleeding, or pain is the warning sign. Other complications include pathologic fracture through weakened bone, growth disturbance and limb length discrepancy when the physis is damaged, septic arthritis by extension, bacteremia with endocarditis, epidural abscess in vertebral disease, and reactive systemic AA amyloidosis from years of chronic inflammation, in which the liver produces serum amyloid A that deposits in the kidney and other organs.

blocks.predict: Why does chronic osteomyelitis often relapse even after the patient's inflammatory markers have returned to normal?
blocks.explain: Bacteria survive in the avascular sequestrum and in biofilm, where neutrophils, antibody, and circulating drugs cannot reach them. With little active inflammation, ESR and CRP can fall while viable organisms remain and later reactivate.
blocks.check: The flow figure and the paragraph on the sequestrum.

blocks.text: Gangrene is a clinical term, not a separate type of necrosis. It describes necrosis of a limb, usually the lower leg, that has lost its blood supply. Which pattern of necrosis it shows depends on whether protein denaturation or enzymatic digestion dominates.

Dry gangrene follows slowly progressive arterial occlusion, most often atherosclerotic peripheral artery disease. Ischemia and acidosis denature structural proteins and also the cell's own enzymes, so dead cells cannot digest themselves and the tissue keeps its outline: coagulative necrosis. Without blood flow the tissue dries, mummifies, and turns black as hemoglobin breaks down. Living tissue at the edge mounts acute inflammation, forming a sharp line of demarcation between dead and viable tissue. Because there is little moisture and few bacteria, spread is slow and systemic toxicity is minimal.

Wet gangrene develops when bacteria infect the dead tissue, or when venous outflow is also blocked so the tissue stays swollen and moist. Neutrophils recruited by the infection release hydrolytic enzymes, and bacterial enzymes add to them, so the tissue is digested: liquefactive necrosis superimposed on the coagulative pattern. The limb is swollen, moist, foul smelling, and poorly demarcated, the infection spreads along tissue planes, and bacteremia and sepsis can follow.

blocks.title: Dry and wet gangrene compared
rows: Arterial or venous compromise plus bacterial infection
blocks.caption: Infection converts a stable, demarcated lesion into a spreading, toxic one.

blocks.text: Diabetes raises the risk of both forms through several converging mechanisms. Atherosclerosis is accelerated and tends to involve the smaller infrapopliteal arteries diffusely, which limits collateral flow. Microangiopathy with basement membrane thickening and hyaline arteriolosclerosis impairs nutrient and oxygen exchange. Sensory neuropathy lets pressure injuries go unnoticed, autonomic neuropathy dries and cracks the skin, and hyperglycemia impairs neutrophil adhesion, chemotaxis, phagocytosis, and oxidative killing while glucose-rich tissue supports bacterial growth. A small wound in an ischemic, insensate foot therefore progresses readily from ulcer to infection to wet gangrene. Smoking, hypertension, and dyslipidemia add to peripheral artery disease in people without diabetes, and gangrene typically begins in the toes, the most distal territory.

Gas gangrene is rapidly progressive necrosis of skeletal muscle caused by toxin-producing clostridia, most often Clostridium perfringens (type A). Clostridia are large, gram-positive, spore-forming anaerobic rods found in soil and the intestinal tract. The classic setting is a deep, contaminated wound with devitalized muscle: crush and battlefield injuries, compound fractures, gunshot wounds, and contaminated surgical wounds, especially of the bowel or biliary tract. Dead tissue, foreign bodies, and impaired blood supply lower the oxygen tension and redox potential, which lets spores germinate. Clostridium septicum causes spontaneous gas gangrene without trauma by spreading from the bowel through the blood, and is associated with colon cancer and neutropenia.

The main virulence factor is alpha toxin, a phospholipase C (lecithinase) that hydrolyzes phosphatidylcholine and sphingomyelin in cell membranes. It lyses muscle cells, red cells, platelets, and leukocytes, and it activates platelets and endothelium so that small vessels thrombose. Theta toxin (perfringolysin O), a cholesterol-dependent pore-forming toxin, adds to cell lysis. Both toxins cause leukocytes to aggregate within vessels at the edge of the lesion, so the necrotic muscle contains strikingly few neutrophils. Necrosis lowers oxygen tension further, so the infection advances along muscle bundles at a rate that can be measured in hours.

blocks.title: How alpha toxin produces the clinical picture
steps: Spores germinate in anaerobic, devitalized muscle
Alpha toxin hydrolyzes membrane phospholipids
Muscle cells lyse; microvessels thrombose
Ischemia extends the anaerobic zone; spread accelerates
Fermentation produces gas in tissue: crepitus
Red cells lyse; toxins depress the heart: shock
blocks.caption: Tissue destruction and the anaerobic environment feed each other.

blocks.text: The clinical features follow this mechanism. Incubation is short, usually under 3 days. Severe pain at the wound, out of proportion to its appearance, is often the first symptom. Fermentation of muscle glycogen and glucose produces hydrogen and carbon dioxide, giving crepitus on palpation and gas within muscle on imaging. The skin changes from pale and tense to a bronze, then purple or black color, with hemorrhagic bullae and a thin, watery, brownish discharge. Necrotic muscle is pale and does not contract or bleed. Gram stain of the discharge shows large boxcar-shaped gram-positive rods with few neutrophils, and spores are rarely seen in tissue. In culture, C. perfringens shows a double zone of hemolysis on blood agar and lecithinase activity on egg yolk agar that antitoxin inhibits (the Nagler reaction).

Systemic toxicity develops quickly. Alpha toxin causes intravascular hemolysis with anemia, hemoglobinuria, and jaundice; it depresses myocardial contractility and, with the cytokines released from dying tissue, causes hypotension and shock. Acute kidney injury follows from hemoglobin and myoglobin pigment and hypoperfusion. Gas in tissue is not unique to clostridia: type I necrotizing fasciitis also produces gas, but it spreads in fascia, while clostridial myonecrosis destroys muscle itself.

blocks.title: Fascia or muscle?
blocks.text: Two days after a crush injury to the thigh with a deep, soil-contaminated wound, a man has severe pain, crepitus, bronze skin with bullae, a thin brown discharge, dark urine, and a falling hematocrit. Gas plus rapid spread could suggest necrotizing fasciitis, so reason from the clues. The deep, devitalized wound gives an anaerobic site for spores. Dark urine with falling hematocrit points to intravascular hemolysis, a hallmark of alpha toxin. A Gram stain showing large gram-positive rods with very few neutrophils fits clostridia, whose toxins keep leukocytes out of the lesion. The diagnosis is clostridial myonecrosis from C. perfringens.

blocks.predict: Why does gas gangrene contain so few neutrophils when ordinary bacterial infections produce pus?
blocks.explain: Alpha and theta toxins lyse leukocytes and make them aggregate inside vessels at the margin of the lesion, and thrombosed vessels cannot deliver them, so the dead muscle has little inflammatory infiltrate.
blocks.check: The paragraph on alpha toxin and the flow figure.

blocks.text: Healthy skeletal muscle resists bacterial seeding even during bacteremia, so infection usually needs a predisposing factor. Pyomyositis is a primary abscess within a large skeletal muscle, most often the quadriceps, gluteal muscles, or iliopsoas. Staphylococcus aureus causes most cases, with group A streptococci less often. Once called tropical pyomyositis, it now occurs in temperate regions, especially with HIV infection, diabetes, malignancy, immunosuppression, injection drug use, and recent muscle injury or strenuous exercise, which may give circulating bacteria a damaged site to seed.

The course has three stages. In the invasive stage the muscle is firm, swollen, and only mildly tender, with low fever. In the suppurative stage, about 10 to 21 days later, an abscess forms, with fever, marked tenderness, and pus on aspiration. In the late stage, untreated infection causes bacteremia and septic shock. Because the abscess is deep, the overlying skin may look nearly normal. Creatine kinase is often normal or only mildly elevated because the necrosis is localized, unlike in diffuse myositis. Ultrasound, CT, or MRI shows the abscess. An iliopsoas abscess can also be secondary, spreading from vertebral osteomyelitis, Pott disease, Crohn disease, or appendicitis, and causes flank pain with pain on hip extension.

Trichinellosis (trichinosis) is caused by the nematode Trichinella spiralis and related species. People ingest larvae encysted in undercooked meat, classically pork and wild game such as bear, wild boar, and walrus. Gastric acid and pepsin free the larvae, which invade the small intestinal epithelium and mature into adults within about a week. Females are viviparous and release newborn larvae for several weeks; these enter lymphatics and blood and invade striated muscle, especially active, well perfused muscles such as the diaphragm, masseter, tongue, extraocular, intercostal, and limb muscles. Each larva enters a single muscle cell and reprograms it into a nurse cell with a collagen capsule and a new capillary network, where it coils and can survive for years before calcifying. Larvae also enter cardiac muscle and the brain but do not encyst there.

blocks.title: Life cycle of Trichinella spiralis in humans
steps: Encysted larvae eaten in undercooked pork or game
Stomach acid frees larvae; they invade small bowel
Adults mate; females release newborn larvae
Larvae spread through lymph and blood
Larvae invade striated muscle cells
Nurse cell encapsulates a coiled larva; later calcifies
blocks.caption: Humans are dead-end hosts: the cycle continues only when another animal eats the encysted muscle.

blocks.text: Symptoms follow the two phases. The intestinal phase, in the first week, brings nausea, diarrhea, and abdominal pain, and may be mild. The muscle phase, beginning about the second week, brings fever, myalgia, muscle tenderness and weakness, periorbital and facial edema, conjunctival hemorrhages, and subungual splinter hemorrhages. These findings reflect an immune and vascular reaction to migrating larvae and their antigens, with inflammation of small vessels and capillary leak. Tissue invasion by a helminth drives a Th2 response: IL-5 produces marked eosinophilia, which peaks around weeks 2 to 4, and IL-4 increases IgE. Muscle cell injury raises creatine kinase and lactate dehydrogenase. Myocarditis, encephalitis, and pneumonitis are the serious complications, and myocarditis is the main cause of death.

blocks.title: Pyomyositis and trichinellosis compared
rows: Hematogenous seeding, often of injured muscle
Firm swelling, then fluctuant abscess, fever
blocks.caption: Neutrophils mark the bacterial abscess; eosinophils mark the migrating helminth.

integration.text: Anatomy of the blood supply ties this chapter together. Fenestrated synovial capillaries without a basement membrane make the joint easy to seed; looping metaphyseal vessels make the growing child's long bone the target of hematogenous osteomyelitis, while avascular adult discs push infection into the vertebral endplate; perforating vessels through the fascia explain why skin necrosis lags behind necrotizing fasciitis; and arterial occlusion turns a toe into dry gangrene. Pathology then describes the response: liquefactive necrosis where neutrophils and bacterial enzymes digest tissue, coagulative necrosis where ischemia alone kills, and the avascular sequestrum that lets chronic bone infection persist.

Microbiology and immunology explain the speed and severity. Staphylococcal adhesins and biofilm favor bone, joints, and implants; streptococcal superantigens cause toxic shock; clostridial phospholipase destroys membranes and keeps neutrophils out; and a tissue-invading helminth produces eosinophilia instead of pus. Host factors, particularly diabetes, sickle cell disease, and terminal complement deficiency, explain who is affected. The limits of testing matter as much as the findings: Gram stains miss many joint infections, radiographs lag by about two weeks, and inflammatory markers are sensitive but not specific, so culture of joint fluid or bone remains the definitive evidence.

summary: Septic arthritis is mostly hematogenous because synovium is highly vascular with no basement membrane; S. aureus is most common and N. gonorrhoeae is classic in sexually active young adults.
Neutrophil proteases and IL-1 driven metalloproteinases destroy avascular cartilage within days, and lost cartilage is not replaced.
Synovial fluid: noninflammatory under 2,000 WBC/mm3, inflammatory about 2,000 to 50,000, septic usually over 50,000 with over 75% neutrophils and low glucose; crystals do not exclude infection.
Urate crystals are needle shaped and negatively birefringent; calcium pyrophosphate crystals are rhomboid and weakly positively birefringent.

Necrotizing fasciitis spreads along fascia and thromboses perforating vessels, so pain is out of proportion to the skin; type I is polymicrobial with gas, type II is group A streptococcus with superantigen toxic shock.

Childhood hematogenous osteomyelitis seeds the metaphysis, where looping vessels slow flow; adult hematogenous disease is vertebral and involves two vertebrae and the disc, and diabetic foot disease spreads from contiguous ulcers.
Raised pressure and periosteal stripping create a sequestrum and involucrum; MRI is the most sensitive imaging, and chronic sinus tracts can develop squamous cell carcinoma.
Dry gangrene is coagulative necrosis from arterial occlusion with sharp demarcation; wet gangrene adds infection and liquefactive necrosis and can cause sepsis.
Clostridium perfringens alpha toxin (lecithinase) lyses muscle, red cells, and platelets, producing crepitus, bronze skin, hemolysis, shock, and few neutrophils.
Pyomyositis is an S. aureus abscess in a large muscle; trichinellosis from undercooked pork or game causes myalgia, periorbital edema, and eosinophilia as larvae encyst in muscle.

verify: Synovial fluid cutoffs vary between sources (inflammatory upper limit given as 50,000, 75,000, or 100,000 WBC/mm3; septic neutrophil threshold 75% to 90%); confirm the values NABNE uses.
Gram stain sensitivity in nongonococcal septic arthritis (about 50%) and blood culture positivity in hematogenous osteomyelitis (about 50%) are approximate and vary among series.
Some sources add a type III necrotizing fasciitis (Vibrio vulnificus or clostridial) and a type IV (fungal); confirm whether NABNE tests this extended classification.
